7.10.m: Sanatkumāra said: / When that army was being struck down thus by Soma of matchless splendour, / the great sorcerer, the asura Hiraṇyākṣa, son of Diti, took heart then and, filled with rage, / addressed the valiant son of Garuḍa, his charioteer in battle: / "O king of birds, have you no shame here in the ocean of battle, / that today you carry me away from the conflict in the chariot to another place? / What will all the asuras and the mighty daityas say? / 'Our king, the tormentor of enemies, has been defeated in battle by the foes; / seeking to save his life, that evil-minded one has abandoned us, his children, / and fled somewhere from the battle.' Fie upon me, the worker of evil! / Having become the son of Kaśyapa, the esteemed brother of the daitya / Hiraṇyakaśipu, a daitya endowed with the power of great yoga, / at the forefront of all the daityas and the dānavas likewise, / king, master, and hero—how could he be conquered by enemies? / Or perhaps you belong to the side of the gods, being indeed the son of Garuḍa; / you serve that very faction and do not protect me!"

Then, having pierced him in the forehead, those two gods, the Moon and Fire, / raised a loud roar, O Vyāsa, like clouds at the end of the world-age. / Seeing their swift dexterity, the glorious Hiraṇyākṣa / neutralized that cold with a supreme fiery missile. / Having burned that shower of frost, he then again by sorcery, / after causing delusion, swiftly became Rāhu and charged forth. (25–27)
Being swallowed then by that Rāhu, the lord of birds, / abandoning the battle, went elsewhere; then the Daitya roared. // But when that cold-store [moon] vanished, all those Dānavas, / regaining breath, fought once more against the hosts of gods. / Roaring like thunderous clouds, resounding like the ocean, // those great chariot-warriors of the Daityas and Dānavas, the foremost riders, recovering, / […] eager for battle, were like tusked great elephants dwelling in the forest. // Thus ends the ninety-first chapter on the battle in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.10.m:
The best among the Vasus, assuming a fierce form, / burned their manifold armors and heads, making all directions resound. / While they cried out 'Alas, alas!' there, the Lord Bearer of Oblations, / burning with his tongue, O Vyāsa, shone like a lamp stationed in a cave. / Burning the faces of some of the Dānavas, / like blooming lotuses, that enemy of darkness possessed great radiance.
The Lord Fire burned the gold-adorned trunks / of some foremost elephants, like a forest fire burning serpents. / The Lord Fire burned arrows and bows, / as well as sword-trappings, elephants, and horses completely everywhere. / Being slain, disarmed, and intensely tormented, / their armor stripped off, those Daitya leaders wandered about hither and thither.
As those enemies of the gods, inflamed by the fire, were burning, / King Hiraṇyākṣa himself became a rain-cloud.

By that sound, by signals, and by proclaiming names, / as well as by touch of hands, they then sent one another to the abode of Yama. / Neither god nor Daitya nor Dānava could be recognized there; / being unable to distinguish, they made this arrangement there: / The Daityas uttered 'Āṭi', and the gods uttered 'Baka'; / those who said 'Baka', the Daityas slew them then; / and the gods [slew] whoever said 'Āṭi'—thus it went on. / Such was the battle that lasted for a thousand years, / causing great fear indeed among the Daityas with the gods in the darkness. / Then, in that darkness, an exceedingly terrifying, extremely dreadful battle took place, / destructive to the world, shedding torrents of blood between the gods and the Asuras who wished for the welfare of the world.
Thus ends the ninety-second chapter in the War [section] of the Skandapurāṇa.

Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard his words, all those seers,
O Vyāsa, spoke again to that powerful Hiraṇyākṣa: 19
The ṛṣis said:
'For the sake of the functioning of the world's order, O foremost of daityas, / all this was made by Brahmā long ago, and dharma was also set in motion.
And considering this world, dharma was set in motion; / let it not be rendered non-existent, O daitya: thus be a grantor of a boon to us.
That vow of yours would prevail, which is the removal of suffering for the worlds, / and therefore Brahmā's imperishable creation would not perish.

7.10.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Having heard their speech and considering the ṛṣis, the daitya king said:
'Those who are treacherous, siding with Indra, and breakers of my command—
death and torments in the hells shall belong only to them.' / This the king said then, and they too said to the ruler of men:
'So be it,' and saying [this] to them, he ordered release from torment. / Having released all the hell-dwellers, he gave the protection of the post
to the king of the ancestors, the sinless and mighty Vipracitti. / Then, proclaiming victory and having honored those twice-born, / the mighty Hiraṇyākṣa went to the dwelling of the Lord of Wealth.
Making that city of the Lord of Wealth resound, the exceedingly powerful dānavas, guarded by Andhaka, / surrounding Hiraṇyākṣa, then rushed forward like clouds toward a mountain.
Thus ends the ninety-fourth chapter, named 'The Departure to the World of Yama', in the conquest of the quarters by Hiraṇyākṣa in the Skandapurāṇa.

No wicked conduct existed in the kingdom while he ruled the realm. / He himself was the wind, the moon, and the sun,
 endowed with the power of tapas among the worlds, O Vyāsa. / Plants sprouted by themselves while that king ruled;
 without plowing, they thrived, providing for all the people. / Taking them, the Daitya king himself brought them to maturity;
 he himself threshed them and brought them back to the households. / He himself was the punisher, and he indeed was the punishment.
 Through his mastery he continually guarded against thieves everywhere. / In his [kingdom], no one fell ill, nor did anyone die,
 nor was anyone attached to another's wife, nor was anyone ever a slanderer. / In his [realm] there were no violent people, nor were there ever the unrighteous.
Ponds, lakes, rivers, and waterfalls / arose everywhere in fine condition even without rain.
In his realm there were no rākṣasas, nor injurious piśācas; / there were no pestilences, nor were there any dualities.
Brahmins did not offer into the fire at that time, while that king [ruled]; / they did not study, nor did they sacrifice; there was then a single caste.
Those who were Bhṛgu brahmins, bringing joy to the Dānavas, / studied and sacrificed everywhere in that manner, O Vyāsa.
All was joyful and thriving, free from sickness and sorrow, / devoid of the classes and stages of life, a world where all people were equal.

Vyāsa said:
While that king, the Daitya ruler, was thus the lord over the three worlds, auspiciously, / and the earth had been bound, and the subjects were happy,
what did the gods do, fallen from their stations, displaced, endowed with great power, / and afflicted with sorrow? Recount this to me in full.
Sanatkumāra said:
Hear what the condition of the gods became, / and what all of them, afflicted with sorrow, did in order.
Fire, the carrier of oblations, had been the increaser of the gods' share. / Having cast him out, the Daitya produced another fire.
In that ritual, O best of brahmins, the mantras followed along with him, / declaring the shares of the Daityas and Dānavas and securing good fortune.
Then the Sacrifice in person attended upon the great-souled Daityas. / And when the Sacrifice had gone over to the Daitya leaders, all the gods were as if dead;
they lost consciousness, their energy and prowess grew faint, / they were stripped of fortune, deprived of effort, having none to call to, filled with distress,

7.10.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed thus by Brahmā, the lords of the gods, having obtained yoga, / bowed to the creator of all beings and spoke this: / "Our places of great yoga have been seized by the sons of Diti. / Tell us where we are to stay; direct us to an imperishable abode." / Brahmā said:
"All your abodes have been seized, and this is known to me. / Listen to where you must dwell by means of your power of yoga: / enter with yoga into the bodies of all the creatures, / everywhere, O best of gods; from that you will obtain sustenance. / By their food and drink, and by various bodily rites, / the earth, even though held by the Nāga, will nourish you." / Sanatkumāra said:
Addressed in this way by the god, all the gods, along with Indra, / did just as Brahmā, the grandfather of the worlds, had said. / Staying there, the best of gods maintained themselves continually, / serving through the four ages, abiding by the design of the Creator of the world. / Then, through yoga, Hiraṇyākṣa saw the gods stationed within creatures; / possessed of yoga, he grew furious with them. / Wherever he saw a god abiding, / the best of the Dānavas approached and struck down that very one.

Hearing those words of the frightened dwellers of heaven, / the Blessed Brahmā spoke to all the gods: / "You must not fear that yogin, that great-souled one, O gods! / All the fruit of that Daitya's austerity has come to an end. / His time has arrived, O gods, which will bring an end to his life; / therefore, all of you go with me and pray to Viṣṇu.
"For today you are powerless and incapable of afflicting him; / Viṣṇu is capable, and he will divest that Daitya of his life.
"For formerly, when he was born, a bodiless voice declared: / 'This one cannot be slain by a man, nor in any way by a god,
"'nor by one born among animals, nor on earth, nor in fire, / nor in the sky, nor in the worlds; great shall this one be.'
"O gods, this lord of the Daityas, who was then great and righteous, / invulnerable to all beings, will now be slain with great effort.

Sanatkumāra said:
[…]
always honoring the tigers among the gods, he spoke this:
"From here that foolish Daitya, having allies, hates the gods.
Let a mortal form be made for me; let me assume a boar's nature.
That lord of the Daityas is great-souled, powerful, and righteous;
he cannot be killed by me alone—I speak the truth to you.
Assuming a boar form consisting of all the gods, increasing joy,
I shall kill that mighty lord of the Daityas.
In that form for all of us, O best of the gods,
Brahmā takes on the role of the Brahman priest, and Yama that of the leader;
Varuṇa there is the Udgātṛ singer, and then Hiraṇyākṣa is the sacrificial animal;
I am the slaughterer, O best of the gods, [and] his fame is mighty.
Today let all beings see between me and him, both of us,
[…]
like two rutting elephants in the forest for the sake of a female."
Hearing that speech of his and the roar of the great-souled one,
their eyes blossoming with joy, looking at one another,
they considered the exceedingly powerful Daitya lord as already slain.
For them, the radiant gaze resembling a blossoming lotus shone most beautifully:
just as in ancient times his mighty guru was slain by the one whose form was Narasiṃha.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter in the Skandapurāṇa, named 'The Means for the Slaying of Hiraṇyākṣa'.

7.10.m:
"Go in your ten thousands, O mighty ones, to him!
Find out who he is, and then I myself will proceed." (67)
Addressed thus, all those master illusionists went forth delighted,
infantry armed and ready, their finger-guards of monitor-lizard skin strapped on. (68)
Those mighty sons of Dānavas and Daityas, wearing bright gold ornaments, garments, and necklaces,
roaring in many ways, exceedingly enraged, went forth just like venomous serpents. (69)
Thus ends the hundredth chapter, entitled "The Dispatch of the Kiṅkaras", in the Skandapurāṇa.

7.10.m:
Sanatkumāra said:
Setting forth with speed, the mail-clad Daityas and Dānavas
marched against the Boar like distressed deer against a lion. (1)
Those lords of Asuras, being drawn on by the gaze of the Boar,
appeared, O Vyāsa, ready in armor like sacrificial animals that have been consecrated. (2)
Having bound them with cords of death by the dispenser of doom,
he led those Daityas along at that time as a man leads animals. (3)
Having traversed eight yojanas, they all beheld the Boar
who had emerged from the ocean's waters, like small beasts [beholding] a lion. (4)
Having looked at him for a moment, the infuriated Daityas and Dānavas
surrounded him on every side, stretching their bows. (5)
